law.jurisdiction: Local — SF Rent Ordinance (Admin. Code ch. 37)
law.rule: Most residential units built on or before June 13, 1979 are rent controlled. The 1940 building qualifies (not a single-family dwelling).
Landlord may raise rent only by the Rent Board's annual percentage, once every 12 months. 60% of the Bay Area CPI-U change.
Published allowable increases for recent periods.
Increase is calculated on base rent only (incl. housing services such as parking/storage; excl. temporary passthroughs). Rent increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar.
First increase 12 months after lease began; each increase sets a new anniversary date; no second increase within 12 months.

30-day written notice; 90-day written notice if the increase alone or combined with another increase in the same year exceeds 10%; +5 days if mailed. Notice should state dollar amount, percentage, and effective date; use the rate in effect on the effective date.

Landlord must report into the Rent Board Housing Inventory (annual deadline March 1) and hold a current rent increase license before any annual or banked increase goes into effect; a notice is not enforceable without a license on the effective date.

A skipped increase is banked only if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase; no limit on the banked amount; cannot be compounded or prorated; does not expire during the tenancy; does not carry to a new tenant; notice must state the banked portion.
No limit on the rent first charged when renting an empty rent-controlled unit to a new tenant.
Landlord cannot charge additional rent simply because a new/additional roommate moved in; such a charge is an unlawful rent increase.
Increases beyond the annual allowable amount are possible only through landlord petitions and passthroughs (e.g., capital improvements, operating costs) under Rent Board rules.

law.jurisdiction: State — CA Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482), Civ. Code §1947.12
law.rule: Over any 12-month period, gross rental rate may not increase more than 5% plus the regional CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, measured against the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months; max two increments per 12 months. Units under a stricter local ordinance are exempt from the state cap (local cap controls).
CA AG chart: San Francisco Area (Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo) maximum under AB 1482. Not the operative cap for these units — the lower local 1.6% AGA controls.

Written notice at least 30 days before effective date for increases of 10% or less (alone or combined with increases in the prior 12 months); at least 90 days if more than 10%; personal delivery or mail under CCP §1013 (+5 days when mailed within California).

§3604(b): unlawful to discriminate in the terms, conditions, or privileges of rental of a dwelling because of race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin. Uniform, consistently applied rent-increase practices are the defensible standard.
No federal statute capping residential rent increases was located in the official sources checked; federal law relevant to increases is the anti-discrimination Fair Housing Act. See flag R-F5.

answers.question: What is a reasonable and normal rental increase for these units (94122) under local, state, and federal law?
answers.answer: Local (controls): the SF Rent Board annual allowable increase — 1.6% for effective dates 3/1/2026-2/28/2027 (60% of Bay Area CPI-U) — once per 12 months. Unit 1: +$63.92 to $4,058.92; Unit 2: +$50.40 to $3,200.40. State: AB 1482 caps at 8.8% for the SF Area for increases starting 8/1/2026-7/31/2027, but the lower local cap governs these rent-controlled units. Federal: no rent cap; only anti-discrimination rules. Anything above the local AGA needs a Rent Board petition.

answers.question: How do big real estate corporations handle increases vs. individual owners in SF?
answers.answer: The same ordinances apply to every owner regardless of size — the SF Rent Ordinance and AB 1482 do not distinguish corporate from individual landlords (AB 1482's only ownership-based exemption is for non-corporate single-family homes). Both must hold a rent increase license, follow the AGA, and give proper notice. Claims about differing internal market practices of large firms are not verifiable from official sources — see flag R-F4.

answers.question: What is the correct way to inform tenants of an increase, and what are reasonable reasons?
answers.answer: Written notice at least 30 days before the effective date (90 days if >10% combined in the year; +5 days if mailed), stating the dollar amount, percentage, effective date and any banked portion, using the rate in effect on the effective date, with a current rent increase license on file. The standard, reasonable reason is the annual CPI-based allowable increase; above-cap amounts require a Rent Board petition (capital improvements / operating-cost passthroughs).

answers.question: Will the increase survive scrutiny by SF tenant advocates / free tenant lawyers?
answers.answer: It is designed to: 1.6% is the published allowable increase, notice and licensing rules are followed, and both units are treated identically. Tenants have free resources — Rent Board counseling (415-252-4600) and Prop F Right to Counsel via the Eviction Defense Collaborative. Have a SF tenant-rights attorney review the actual notice before serving; this site is not legal advice.

answers.question: Raise one unit or both — discrimination risk?
answers.answer: Raise both units with the same lawful percentage and identical procedure. The federal Fair Housing Act (§3604(b)) prohibits discrimination in the terms and conditions of rental; singling out one unit without a documented, lawful, uniformly applied reason creates disparate-treatment risk. Uniform application is the defensible normal business practice.
